content: 1. Transplacental Transmission of Ebola Virus: A rare case of Ebola virus transmission through the placenta was documented, highlighting the potential for vertical transmission during pregnancy. (Okoror et al., 2018) 2. Persistence and Genetic Stability of Ebola Virus: During the 1995 Kikwit outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo, the Ebola virus demonstrated genetic stability and persistence, which has implications for understanding its transmission dynamics. (Rodriguez et al., 1999) 3. Ebola Virus Persistence in Body Fluids: (Ebola Virus Persistence Study Group, 2016) 4. Clinical and Laboratory Follow-Up of an Ebola Patient: A comprehensive follow-up of a female Ebola survivor in Sierra Leone revealed insights into the persistence of the virus and its clinical implications. (Liu et al., 2019) 5. Risk of Ebola Virus Transmission from Bodily Fluids and Fomites: Research assessed the risk of Ebola virus transmission through contact with bodily fluids and contaminated surfaces, underscoring the importance of strict infection prevention protocols. (Bausch et al., 2007) 6. Ebola Virus in Breast Milk: A study in Guinea documented the presence of the Ebola virus in the breast milk of an infected mother with twin babies, raising concerns about breastfeeding safety during active infection. (Nordenstedt et al., 2016) 7. Persistence of Ebola Virus in Breast Milk: Another study identified breast milk as a potential source of Ebola virus transmission from mother to child, even after the mother showed no symptoms of illness. (Sissoko et al., 2017) 8. Rapid Sequencing of Ebola Virus: During the Sierra Leone outbreak, rapid sequencing of the Ebola virus helped identify transmission chains linked to sporadic cases, aiding in outbreak control efforts. (Arias et al., 2016) 9. Management of Pregnant and Breastfeeding Women with Ebola: Guidelines emphasize the need for specialized care for pregnant and breastfeeding women with Ebola, including safe delivery practices, infection prevention, and counseling on breastfeeding risks. (WHO, 2018) 10. Impact of Maternal Illness on Young Children: A study explored the effects of maternal Ebola illness and breastfeeding on the risk of disease transmission to very young children. (Bower et al., 2016) 11. Transmission and Risk Factors in Uganda: Research on Ebola hemorrhagic fever in Uganda identified key risk factors for transmission among contacts, providing valuable insights for outbreak management. (Francesconi et al., 2003) 12. Lactating Mothers Infected with Ebola: A study suggested that testing only blood samples for Ebola virus in lactating mothers may be insufficient, as the virus can persist in breast milk. (Moreau et al., 2015) 13. Community Isolation During Ebola Outbreak: (Williams et al., 2015) 14. Follow-Up of Ebola Contacts in the DRC: Clinical, virologic, and immunologic follow-up of Ebola survivors and their households in Kikwit, DRC, provided insights into post-recovery virus dynamics. (Rowe et al., 1999) 15. Viremia and Virus Secretion in Survivors: A cross-sectional study in Sierra Leone investigated viremia and virus secretion in Ebola survivors, contributing to understanding the long-term effects of the disease. (Green et al., 2016) 16. Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome After Plasma Use: A case in Spain reported acute respiratory distress syndrome following the use of convalescent plasma in treating an Ebola patient, highlighting potential complications. (Mora-Rillo et al., 2015) 17. Management of Ebola in the United States: A cluster of three Ebola cases in the U.S., including the first domestically acquired case, provided insights into clinical management and infection control. (Liddell et al., 2015) 18. Asymptomatic Shedding of Ebola Virus: A case of an asymptomatic pregnant woman shedding the Ebola virus was reported, raising concerns about silent transmission risks. (Akerlund et al., 2015) 19. Evaluation of Ebola Vaccine Safety: The Sierra Leone trial assessed the safety and tolerability of the rVSV-ZEBOV-GP vaccine during the West Africa outbreak, contributing to vaccine development efforts. (Samai et al., 2018) 20. WHO Guidelines on Pregnancy and Ebola: The World Health Organization has issued comprehensive guidelines for managing pregnancy, labor, and breastfeeding in the context of Ebola, emphasizing infection prevention and maternal care. (WHO, 2018) 21. Induced Labor and Pregnancy Complications: (WHO, 2018) 22. Breastfeeding and Ebola: Women with acute or recovered Ebola who choose not to breastfeed due to transmission risks may be offered lactation suppression medications or instructed on safe milk disposal. Breast milk substitutes should meet safety and sustainability criteria. (WHO, 2018) 23. Investigational Therapies for Pregnant Women with Ebola: Limited evidence exists on the efficacy of investigational therapies (e.g., ZMapp, REGN-EB3, remdesivir) in improving maternal or neonatal outcomes in pregnant women with Ebola. (WHO, 2018) 24. Induced Abortion During Ebola: Evidence is insufficient to determine whether induced abortion during acute Ebola improves maternal survival or reduces disease severity. However, it may theoretically reduce viral load and transmission risks. (WHO, 2018) 25. Ethical Considerations in Ebola Management: Ethical guidelines emphasize the importance of balancing maternal and fetal outcomes, respecting patient autonomy, and ensuring safe practices for healthcare providers. (WHO, 2016) This transformation provides a clear and professional summary of the key findings and recommendations related to Ebola virus disease in the context of pregnancy, breastfeeding, and maternal care.
